title_content.content: Who pays for Electrification and Artificial Intelligence?

paragraph_content.content: We explore the cost of electrifying Europe and of rolling out datacenters to support artificial intelligence. Our analysis suggests that electricity bill increases over the coming ten years will be much lower than anticipated, averaging 2-4% pa. This should ease concerns over affordability-driven regulatory intervention and strongly corroborates our thesis of an “earnings super cycle” in Utilities and ongoing multiple expansion.

Even with electrification and AI, power bill growth would be just 2-4% pa. Over the past ten years, power bills for a typical European household have increased by +5% pa. Over the coming ten years, we estimate that electricity bills will increase at a slower pace, despite accelerating electrification and rising AI adoption. Our base case (EU targets largely missed, slow DC roll-out) implies +2% annual growth in bills, while our hyper-adoption scenario for electrification and datacenters increases this to +4% pa. These figures are significantly below prevailing expectations and reflect two common misconceptions about capex and power demand.

North vs South divide. We estimate that annual electricity bill increases could reach the mid-to-high single digits in the UK and Germany, driven primarily by rising grid fees, although Germany may be better positioned to mitigate the impact through fiscal support. In Italy and Spain, we forecast largely unchanged power bills until 2035, supported by more modest grid-fee growth and normalizing power prices.

About 35-40% of electrification capex is non-inflationary or deflationary. We estimate c.35-40% of investments in the power system over the coming ten years (€2.2-3.5 trn on our two scenarios) will be non-inflationary (eg power grids' maintenance) or deflationary (eg onshore renewable additions, as seen in Spain).

Power demand growth should reduce unit fixed costs. Rising power consumption from new sources – EVs, heat pumps, industrial electric boilers, aircon, datacenters – should spread fixed costs (eg grid fees) over a larger base, thereby reducing unit costs. In our base case, we forecast power demand growth of c.1.5-2.5% pa until 2030, accelerating to c.3-3.5% thereafter. Our hyper-adoption scenario (EU goals being met, higher AI Agents penetration) implies 4.5-5% growth from 2030.

Household energy spending could fall by -30%. We estimate electrifying a typical household could lead to c.30% savings in fuel costs – equivalent to an annual reduction in energy costs of €1,200 per family. Given these benefits, policymakers may seek to encourage switching to help alleviate the burden of upfront costs.

Many investors worry that the scale of infrastructure investment required for electrification (€2.2-3.5 trn over the next decade on our estimates) could create affordability challenges, ultimately derailing our organic growth/earnings super-cycle re-rating thesis for the sector. Our analysis, based on both a base-case and a hyper-adoption scenario for electrification and datacentres, suggests these concerns are overstated. On these two scenarios, we estimate electricity bill increases over the coming ten years will average between +2% and +4% pa, respectively. These figures are significantly below prevailing expectations, and also lower than the +5% annual increase in electricity bills, experienced by European consumers over the past ten years. As a result, we believe the electrification process is likely to prove much more manageable from both a social and economic perspective than many investors anticipate. Two factors underpin this seemingly counter-intuitive conclusion: (1) not all capex is inflationary: c.35-40% of the electrification investments that we project are non-inflationary (eg maintenance of power grids) or deflationary (eg onshore renewable additions), and (2) power consumption growth from new sources would lower unit fixed costs, such as grid fees. In our view, these findings strongly support our thesis of an “earnings super cycle” in Utilities and ongoing multiple expansion.

title_content.content: Electrification: 2-4% growth in bills pa, much lower than anticipated

paragraph_content.content: Over the past ten years, the main cost items for a typical European household — housing, food and energy — have increased by +4% pa on average. Electricity bills have risen at an annual rate of +5%. Over the coming ten years, we estimate that electricity bills will increase at a slower rate of between 2% pa and 4% pa based on two scenarios: (1) our base case, which assumes a slower pace of electrification (c.40-50% below EU electrification goals) alongside a gradual datacenters roll out (lagging the US by more than five years), and (2) our hyper-adoption scenario, where we simulate faster electrification (in line with EU goals on EVs and HPs) and stronger adoption rates for AI Agents, requiring a more substantial expansion of datacenter infrastructure. This projected evolution in electricity bills is much lower than commonly perceived, and hence we believe the electrification process is likely to prove much more manageable from both a social and economic perspective than many investors anticipate. Two factors underpin this conclusion: the share of non-inflationary (eg power grids maintenance) and deflationary capex (onshore wind and solar) is higher than prevailing expectations, and power demand growth from new customers should lower unit fixed costs (eg grid fees).

Households' main cost items have been growing +4% over the past ten years
According to Eurostat, household cost inflation averaged +c.4% CAGR across the main spending categories over the past ten years (2016-25). Electricity and gas bills saw the steepest increase, at 5% and 6% CAGR, respectively, while housing costs increased more moderately at c.2% CAGR.

title_content.content: Electricity bills to grow 2-4% pa to 2035

paragraph_content.content: Our base case power demand forecast implies slow progress on electrification and only a gradual roll-out in datacenters. More specifically, by 2030, electrification would remain c.40–50% below EU targets, and our 2031 datacentre forecast is c.15% below the EUDCA's (already conservative) expectations. Under this scenario, power demand would grow by 1.5–2.5% pa to 2030, rising to 3–3.5% thereafter until 2035 as the pace of electrification and, particularly, datacenters development picks up. We estimate that meeting this demand would require c.€2.2 trn of electrification capex over the coming ten years. Our analysis suggests that this would lead to a +2% annual increase in electricity bills over 2026–35E, for Europe. This is less than half of the annual increase experienced by households over the past ten years.

Our hyper-adoption scenario assumes a stronger pace of electrification and a faster datacenters roll-out. Specifically, we assume adoption rates broadly in line with the EU's 2030 targets for mobility and heating: c.30 mn EVs vs around 10 mn in 2026, and c.60 mn HPs vs around 30 mn in 2026. This would require an acceleration in investments across power grids and, in particular, power generation (renewables, gas plants, batteries). Under this scenario, power demand growth would reach 4.5-5% pa over 2030-35.

title_content.content: Meaningful regional deviations: North vs South divide

paragraph_content.content: At a regional level, outcomes are likely to be relatively heterogeneous. Across both our base-case and hyper-adoption scenarios, we expect electricity bills to rise more rapidly in the UK and Germany. Under our base case, annual bill increases reach +4% and +7% respectively, rising to +5% and +8% under our hyper-adoption scenario. This reflects higher investment requirements in power grids (15-25% annual increase in RAB). Germany may be better positioned to mitigate the impact on consumers given the potential scope for fiscal support measures.

By contrast, we expect the evolution of power bills in Italy and Spain to be more muted. Under both scenarios, we forecast broadly unchanged electricity tariffs through 2035; this reflects the much lower increase in grid fees and, especially for Italy, the projected normalization in power prices which are currently nearly twice the levels seen in Spain.

title_content.content: Electrification capex: c.35-40% is non-inflationary or deflationary

paragraph_content.content: We estimate c.35-40% of the electrification capex projected over the coming ten years (€2.2-3.5 trn on our two scenarios) will be non-inflationary (eg maintenance investments in power grids) or deflationary (onshore wind and solar additions will lower energy prices). This is much higher than many perceive and it is one of the reasons why we project a more muted evolution in power bills than anticipated by investors.

As discussed in previous reports (see here), growing electrification needs are placing increasing pressure on an aging power system. This should drive substantial investment upgrades in power grids, as well as in power generation over the next decade. Power grids are c.40 years old and require a major upgrade to accommodate rising demand from new clients: datacenters, heat pumps, electric vehicles, air conditioning and industrial boilers. We also envisage an acceleration in renewable additions, and rising investments in back-up generation — CCGTs and BESS, to offset asset retirements and support rising consumption.

Our base case implies c.€2.2 trn of investment over 2026-35, rising to c.€3.5 trn under our hyper-adoption scenario, which assumes faster electrification and accelerated datacenter deployment – as detailed in the chapter “Electrification: 2-4% growth in bills pa, much lower than anticipated”.
This new level of investment would represent a c.60–150% increase versus the historical level of €1.4 trn, incurred over the past ten years (2016–25).

title_content.content: Power demand growth would lower unit fixed costs

paragraph_content.content: Rising power consumption from new sources – EVs, heat pumps, industrial electric boilers, aircon, datacenters – would spread fixed costs across a larger base (eg grid fees), thereby reducing unit costs. On our base case, power demand would grow by c.1.5-2.5% pa until 2030, accelerating to c.3-3.5% thereafter. Our hyper-adoption scenario (EU goals being met, higher AI Agents penetration rate) implies 4.5-5% growth from 2030.

Recent data suggest that electrification in Europe is accelerating. In 2025, the region sold more than 2 mn EVs (c.20% share of total vehicle sales) and installed >2.5 mn heat pumps (here and here). As a reference, an EV can roughly double a household's electricity consumption when used as the primary family vehicle, while switching from gas to electric heating can have a much higher effect, provided the HP also provides cooling as well as heating. Combined, 2025 EV sales and heat pump installations are equivalent to adding more than 5 mn households to Europe's power system.

Looking ahead, we expect electricity demand growth to be driven by four factors: (1) modest GDP growth, adjusted for energy efficiency, (2) accelerating electrification of transport and buildings, (3) the gradual roll-out of datacenters, and (4) rising air-conditioning penetration. Together, these factors should drive electricity demand growth in our base case of c.1.5-2.5% CAGR through 2030, accelerating to c.3-3.5% thereafter as electrification and datacenter deployment gather pace, as detailed earlier. We note that despite the supportive top-down outlook, we maintain a conservative approach in our company models, assuming electricity demand growth of c.1.5-2.0%.

paragraph_content.content: Despite this near-tripling in power consumption per family, total energy spending should fall. This can be explained by the superior energy efficiency of EVs and HPs, which lower annual running costs for cars and heating. paragraph_content.content: Investment thesis. We are Buy-rated for three reasons: (1) US renewable activities account for c.65% of the business, and we believe the market underestimates the outlook for industry returns (project IRRs at c.10-11% on GSe and as recently estimated by the main US developers), which we expect could remain the highest in US RES history for another 3-5 years; (2) We see major upside vs Visible Alpha Consensus estimates: our expectations for rising returns and an acceleration in organic capex later in the decade suggest a boost in net profit by +c.90% over 2028-31E to c.€1.0-1.1 bn depending on asset rotation gains. Our net profit estimate is c.20% ahead of Visible Alpha Consensus in 2031; and (3) AI adoption rates: EDPR is highly geared to adoption rates in artificial intelligence — DC deals in the US or Iberia provide scope for valuation upside.

Valuation methodology. Our 12-month price target of €17.50 is based on a combination of: (1) 2/3 to our 2027E SOTP of €20.0/share. We value the core RES Business via a DCF using a 5.8% WACC and model capacity additions through to 2036, with the implied EV/EBITDA multiple equating to 15.4x; and (2) 1/3 to our valuation of existing assets of €13/share. When valuing the existing assets, we assume no growth beyond 2026. We use an EV/IC approach to derive the valuation of existing assets.

Key risks. Key downside risks to our view and price target include: (1) potential delays in the electrification process in the US/Europe; (2) lower-than-expected capacity additions; (3) lower-than-expected power prices; (4) higher sovereign interest rates; and (5) significant appreciation in foreign currencies (USD/BRL).

Investment thesis. We are Buy-rated for three reasons: (1) Organic growth is under-appreciated: as detailed here, we believe the market is overlooking Enel's return to organic growth, supported by high single digit growth in RAB activities (c.40-45% of EBITDA), annual renewable additions of about +4 GW pa, and the ongoing SBB. This could support mid-single-digit EPS growth to 2030, we estimate; (2) US renewables M&A could prove timely and value enhancing: Our numbers assume c.€12.5 bn of generic re-leveraging for external growth until 2030; this would still keep ND/EBITDA just over 3x, thus implying further B/S headroom with the top end of its target range at 3.5x – we estimate more than €10 bn incrementally. As detailed by management during the Q1 call, US renewables appear in focus – with Enel about to bid (mandatory as well as non binding) on 15 GW of assets in the region; and (3) Highly geared to a re-opening scenario: a re-opening of the Strait of Hormuz could lower sovereign yields (due to lower inflation expectations), while easing affordability concerns (and ad-hoc measures such as energy price caps) owing to normalising power prices.

Valuation methodology. Our 12-month price target is €12.0. It is based on: (1) 1/3 on our SOTP valuation of €12.9/share. We value the RES Business via a DCF using a 6.1% WACC and model capacity additions through 2034. We value the remaining businesses, thermal, hydro, networks, and retail (except for Iberia thermal, where we use a DCF with a c.7% WACC) using an average EV/EBITDA multiple of c.7.5x on 2027E EBITDA; and (2) 2/3 on a 2027E peer-based P/E multiple of 15.2x, a discount vs. the sector of +1 standard deviation and a major discount vs. the current 2027E sector multiples. This implies a valuation of c.€11.8/share.

Key risks. Key downside risks to our thesis and price target: (1) lower commodity/power prices (especially in Iberia and Italy); (2) lower regulated network returns (especially in Italy); (3) lower retail margins in Italy and Iberia; (4) further introduction of regulatory measures that negatively impact profits; (5) higher country risk premia; and (6) sustained depreciation of LatAm.

Investment thesis. Engie trades at a FY2028E P/E of 12.9x (a c.15% discount to the sector) with an EPS CAGR of c.6% pa beyond 2028, on our estimates. We see Engie de-risking in two ways. First, asset rotation and cost-cutting are increasing the share of earnings derived from regulated activities (c.67% by FY 2028E). Second, the group's exposure to commodity price volatility is on track to decline materially by FY2027. This builds a stronger platform to grow the business beyond. Over the medium term, we believe that Engie's strategy should increasingly turn investor focus towards the underlying sum of the parts, helping to unlock embedded value within the portfolio. In parallel, the repositioning of the business towards Renewables, Batteries and Power Networks will focus the portfolio on areas where there is sizable investment opportunity, growth and value. We are Buy-rated, with a 12m price target of €32.6.

Valuation methodology. Our 12-month price target of €32.6 is based on: (1) 65% on a P/E-derived valuation of €32.6/share; and (2) 35% on an SOTP-based valuation of €32.5/share. Our P/E valuation uses a FY 2027E P/E peer average multiple of 16.8x and reflects a 5% sector-relative premium.

Key risks. Key downside risks to our view and price target include: (1) lower commodity prices; (2) weaker-than-expected nuclear output; (3) new “Loi Pacte” allowing the French government to sell down its c.24% stake in Engie; and (4) a weakening EUR against the USD and BRL.

Investment thesis. Our Buy rating is supported by the following factors: (1) EON has seen a significant re-rating since the start of 2025, but it still trades on a 2027 P/E of c.14.5x, in line with the Utilities sector's 10-year mid-cycle. The secular growth in power distribution (2/3 of EON's group EBITDA) is, in our view, likely to support ongoing multiple expansion and continued positive earnings revisions, (2) Increasing capex, supported by a recent German government paper (here), leads us to total 2026-30 investments at c.€53 bn, which compares with current guidance of €48 bn, and (3) EON remains a key electrification enabler, operating nearly 40% of Germany's medium and low voltage grid, and without a major modernization of the power grid, Germany may struggle to electrify its economy and progress its energy security goals. Overall, throughout 2025-30, we estimate an underlying EPS CAGR of +8%.
Valuation methodology. Our 12-month price target of €24 is based on: (1) 1/3 on our SOTP of €26.0/share; and (2) 2/3 on our 2027 P/E valuation of €23/share. This is based on a 17.6x target P/E.

Key risks. Key downside risks to our view and price target include: (1) worse-than-expected network returns; (2) higher refinancing costs; (3) prolonged economic weakness in Germany; and (4) delays in the electrification process in Europe.

Investment thesis. Our Buy rating is underpinned by three core pillars: (1) Major re-leveraging to drive strong earnings revisions: by 2030, we estimate that Naturgy will have €10 bn in re-leveraging potential (see here). Given management's stated growth ambitions, we estimate re-leveraging of €7 bn (our base case) to €10 bn would imply 2030E EPS of €2.58-2.75, implying strong double digit upside vs current Visible Alpha Consensus expectations; (2) Expansion into electricity implies higher multiples: as per management statements, Naturgy seems to favour the acquisition of electricity businesses, which could deliver longer-term organic growth, once acquired. We believe larger exposure to electrification assets could prove positive for multiple expansion. Naturgy continues to trade at a meaningful sector discount; and (3) Near-term upside to profits: the tightness in the LNG market and upside to domestic ancillary profits suggest scope for a near-term earnings beat vs consensus. We expect Naturgy to upgrade its 2026 guidance at the first-half results in the second half of July.
Valuation methodology. Our 12-month price target is €34. It is based on: (1) a P/E valuation (2/3 weight) of €33.3, which uses a target P/E of 15.2x; and (2) an SOTP (1/3 weight) of €34.8/share.

Key risks. Key downside risks to our thesis and price target: (1) lower-than-expected commodity and power prices; (2) higher sovereign interest rates; (3) worse-than-expected macroeconomic conditions, which could have a negative impact on power prices, power demand (due to weaker activity), and credit conditions, while increasing the risks of regulatory intervention; and (4) lower-than-expected EBITDA yield on new investments funded through re-leveraging, which could dilute profitability.

Investment thesis. Nordex is benefiting from the same tailwinds we see driving the broader onshore wind turbine industry. At the top line, improved pricing alongside order growth has supported a recovery of margins. Combined, this creates a picture of higher profits and a stronger balance sheet. We see this translating to higher returns of value over time. This could be used for dividends, buybacks, reserves and for investment into the businesses. We expect further improvement in margins and higher cash returns which, combined with an uptick in onshore US and German orders into this year, sets the stage for the company to achieve its medium-term outlook, and we expect the strong share performance to continue. We are Buy-rated, with a 12m price target of €53.2.
Valuation methodology. Our 12-month price target of €53.2 is based on a DCF valuation, for which we use a 7.9% post-tax WACC in the medium and long term.
Key risks. Key downside risks to our view and price target include: (1) lower global volumes; (2) changes in government policy; and (3) decline in commodity prices.

Investment thesis. Our Buy rating on Orsted is based on three reasons: (1) Europe is pivoting towards electrification and renewables. Following a second energy crunch in less than five years, Europe may increasingly pivot its energy policy towards electrification, leading to much higher power consumption. Utilities – renewables in particular – would be at the core of this process. In a ‘hyper-electrification’ scenario (see here for details), we believe power demand growth would eventually peak at +5% pa later in the decade, while investments in power generation, mostly RES, could triple (vs. 2016-25E) to €2 trn over the coming ten years; (2) US Administration: A softening stance on offshore wind? The US Administration has recently decided not to appeal the injunction on the Sunrise project, thereby allowing Orsted to continue construction (completion is due in summer 2027). While we cannot rule out another government intervention, we believe it is possible that the administration might allow projects already under construction to reach completion; and (3) A strong balance sheet by 2028E: a major opportunity for a turnaround. We estimate that delivering its US projects would push 2028 EBITDA to c.DKK37 bn, without any meaningful capex commitment. We believe that thereafter, the balance sheet could support the development of +1.5 GW pa of new offshore wind, and +c.300 MW of onshore solar/wind. Over 2028-33, we believe this can cumulatively grow EBITDA by +40%, leading to 2033E EBITDA of c.DKK 51 bn, well ahead of Visible Alpha Consensus Data.

Valuation methodology. Our 12-month price target of DKK 190 is based on: (1) 2/3 on our SOTP valuation (Dec-2027E) of DKK 207/share, and; (2) 1/3 on our valuation of Orsted's existing assets derived from an EV/IC approach of DKK 150/share.

Key risks. Key downside risks to our view and price target include: (1) rising pressure on IRRs; (2) further impairments in projects under development; (3) lower success rates on Offshore Wind auctions; (4) construction delays or cost overruns; (5) lower power prices; and (6) significant GBP and/or USD appreciation/depreciation.

Investment thesis. Over the coming five years, PPC is undertaking a material step-up in investment under its strategy to transform into a key leading regional electrification platform, with a target for its installed base set to double within just five years. The plan also marks PPC's entry into the DC infrastructure through a differentiated and highly synergistic business model, giving exposure to a structurally high-growth segment. While our €26.5/sh base case valuation is built on conservative assumptions, successful execution de-risking could support convergence towards our €30/sh Full Execution scenario. At current levels, we view PPC as one of the most attractive entry points into the European electrification growth theme, with exposure to structurally undersupplied power markets with meaningful upside optionality at an undemanding valuation.

Valuation methodology. Our 12-month price target of €26.5 is based on a blend of the following methodologies: (1) SOTP-based valuation (weighting 1/3) of €29.9/share, which combines a DCF approach for the renewables business/power distribution, and market multiples for the remaining businesses; (2) PE-based valuation (weighting 2/3) of €24.6/share, based on average 2028–29E EPS and target multiple based on a sector through-the-cycle PE of 14.5x.

Key risks. Key downside risks to our investment thesis and price target include: (1) lower commodities and power prices; (2) lower-than-assumed renewable and battery additions; (3) lower-than-anticipated returns on new additions; (4) rising competition in the retail market; (5) further delays to the lignite phaseout plan; (6) regulatory intervention; (7) rising interest rates; (8) worse-than-expected macroeconomic conditions.

Investment thesis. We reiterate our Buy rating and €68.5 12-month price target, underpinned by three key drivers: (1) Accelerating electrification: rising energy security needs and improving economics for heat pumps, EVs, and industrial electric boilers are supporting an acceleration in Europe's electrification trend. As supply tends to adjust more slowly to a pick up in power demand, we believe Europe is entering an increasingly attractive environment for renewable returns, similar to that seen in the US. Over time, this should also support stronger RES development; (2) Highly geared to AI and datacenters: the roll-out of datacenters in the US and the substantial evidence that this is also translating to Europe (see here) provide tailwinds to RWE. Selling sites and providing energy could prove value-enhancing (see here). In addition, rising power consumption could drive substantial upside in FlexGen profits (c.€300-600 mn pre-tax upside by 2030-31 under our “hyper-electrification” scenario of +5% demand growth pa in Europe vs our base case, as detailed here); and (3) Amprion strategic pivot may prove a major positive: as detailed here, RWE might be set to increase its stake in the transmission system operator (TSO) Amprion. Although such a step would denote a strategic pivot, we argue that it could prolong ‘earnings growth duration’, lower the cost of capital for the overall business, and potentially turn RWE into an ‘Iberdrola-esque’ company. If properly executed, this could create long-lasting value for shareholders.

Valuation methodology. Our 12-month price target is €68.5. It is based on: (1) 2/3 on our 2027E SOTP of €72.8/share. We value the FlexGen business at a target valuation multiple of 8x and the renewables business using a DCF based on a WACC of 6.1% and on capacity additions until 2035 with no terminal value; and (2) 1/3 on the value of existing assets, at €59.6/share. When valuing existing assets, based on an EV/IC model, we assume no future growth beyond 2026.

Key risks. Key downside risks to our thesis and price target: (1) recession and falling power demand; (2) weaker-than-expected LNG and power prices; (3) higher sovereign interest rates; (4) weak execution in the renewable pipeline; and (5) GBP/USD depreciation.

Investment thesis. We see Siemens Energy's delivery this year as providing reassurance on fundamental demand tailwinds for the business (datacenter demand, grid capex, energy security), and expect further top-line growth and margin improvement. Beyond FY 2028, our estimates imply more than 60% earnings growth through to FY2030, and a further material acceleration in cash flow. This would leave Siemens Energy trading at a c.6x 2030E EV/EBITDA, with visibility and growth expanding. The growth we expect is driven by: (1) higher OEM volumes and stronger service profitability within Gas Service; (2) strong and long-duration top-line growth in Grid Technologies; and (3) increased focus on offshore wind at Siemens Gamesa. Looking at capital returns, we see scope for more than €25bn to be returned to shareholders out to the end of the decade. We continue to see execution narrowing the valuation gap with GE Vernova (covered by Joe Richie), which trades at broadly twice the multiple of Siemens Energy at c.22x 2028E EV/EBITDA. We are Buy-rated, with a 12m price target of €212.

Valuation methodology. Our 12-month price target is €212. Our SOTP-based valuation methodology is based on a peer group CY27E EV/EBITA multiple for Gas & Power of 22.2x. We value Siemens Gamesa using a DCF, in which we use a 7.2% post-tax WACC.

Key risks. Key downside risks to our view and price target include: (1) inability to manage the quality issues emerging in specific onshore wind turbine models; (2) increasing competition and price pressure; (3) failure to deliver cost savings; (4) a weaker economy, and (5) FX and material headwinds.

Investment thesis. We are Buy rated on Snam as we see continuing investment needs over the next decade in the core gas transport business, driven by increasing energy security aspirations in Europe. This should support a

normalised net income CAGR to 2030, with our 2030 forecasts sitting modestly ahead of company targets and consensus. Additional upside could come from post-2029 capex, asset rotation and incremental incentives, not captured in our base case. Yet, the stock trades at an average c.13x P/E over 2027-30 — a double-digit discount to its closest regulated peers. Given Snam's clear core focus, solid growth profile and strong balance sheet, we see this discount as unjustified.

Valuation methodology. Our 12-month price target of €7.10 is based on an equally weighted combination of: (1) An SOTP-based valuation of €7.36/share. In our SOTP, we value the core business using a DCF where we model 10 years of cash flows (until 2035), and a terminal value based on 2035 RAB. We value the associates portfolio using our target P/E for regulated pure play names of 14.5x, which we apply to 2027E earnings; (2) A P/E-based valuation of €7.05/share. Our target P/E is 15.2x, reflecting a sector multiple (in line with our sector view) to which we apply a slight discount given we see the long-term prospects for Snam as slightly lower than for power-exposed names; (3) A target DY-based valuation of €6.86/share, based on a slight premium to the target yield (sector through-the-cycle) of c.5%.

Key risks. Key downside risks to our investment thesis and price target include: (1) lower-than-anticipated capex beyond 2030; (2) lower inflation and interest rates; (3) lower-than-expected regulated incentives; (4) execution risk; (5) higher Italian bond yields, and; (6) further regulatory intervention.

Investment thesis. We believe the market is overlooking the fact that Solaria is the highest-returning (25% ROE by 2028E) renewables developer in our coverage. This is the result, in our view, of better (i.e. higher returning) projects. We also believe that the recent focus on BESS is likely to reduce the risk of “zero pricing” on its merchant exposure. With more DC deals seemingly on the horizon, as recently stated by management, and visible projects that could meaningfully increase the installed base over the coming three years, we believe that successful execution should move Solaria’s valuation steadily higher. Our estimates assume meaningful execution delays but still imply c.9x P/E by 2028E and c.6.5x P/E by 2030E, with a reasonable balance sheet. We remain Buy-rated with a 12m price target of €26.

Valuation methodology. Our 12-month price target of €26 is based on a combination of fundamental (weighted 70%) and M&A valuations (weighted 30%). Our fundamental valuation of €24.5 is based: (1) 2/3 on our SOTP of €27.4/share. We value the core RES & Storage business via a DCF, where we model capacity additions for ten years (until 2035E) and use a 6.6% cost of capital. We value the infrastructure business based on a pure-play EV/EBITDA multiple of 8x and the datacenter business based on the existing pipeline, probability-weighted. (2) 1/3 on our valuation of existing assets of €18.4/share. When valuing existing assets, we assume no growth beyond 2026. The remaining 30% of our price target is based on our M&A-based theoretical valuation of €29.8/share, which is derived from our base-case DCF model and a WACC of 6.1%, as any potential bidder would likely be able to bring more financial solidity to the company's balance sheet, which is reflected through a lower beta and credit spread vs the base case.

Key risks. Key downside risks to our thesis and price target include: (1) lower-than-expected commodity and power prices; (2) execution delays; (3) lower-than-expected returns on new capacity additions; (4) higher sovereign interest rates; and (5) worse-than-expected macroeconomic conditions.

Investment thesis. In our view, Vestas is the best-positioned company in our wind manufacturer coverage, set to benefit from rising wind installation demand, with strong fundamentals (cash flow generation, growth, balance sheet) owing to its geographical diversification and scale. We expect margin expansion over FY 2026, de-risking of the offshore ramp-up and a stronger picture for volume growth through higher order intake. We forecast Vestas to deliver 90% of its medium-term target in FY 2027, largely driven by the offshore business reaching break-even. With Vestas reaching peak offshore wind capital expenditure, we see FCF expansion into FY2027. Combined with new targets for capital structure (between +1x and -1x net debt to EBITDA through-the-cycle) and shareholder returns (at least 40% payout for dividends & buybacks), we expect a step up in returns of value over the coming years. Our estimates assume €5bn in cumulative buybacks between FY2026 and FY2030. We expect further improvement in margins and higher cash returns which, combined with an uptick in onshore US and German orders into this year, sets the stage for a much stronger medium-term outlook and we expect the re-rating to continue. We are Buy-rated, with a 12m price target of Dkr236.

Valuation methodology. Our 12-month price target of Dkr236 is based on a combination of a DCF (85% weighting, Dkr213/share) and an M&A valuation (15% weighting, Dkr364/share). Our DCF-based valuation equates to a target multiple of c.10x 2030E EV/EBIT. For our DCF valuation, we use a 7.8% post-tax WACC in both the medium and long term. Our M&A valuation is derived by applying a 22x multiple to 2030E EBIT (on an ex-IRA growth basis) discounted back to 2026E. Our M&A multiple is based on the second-quartile median average M&A multiple for the Industrials sector in Western Europe over the last ten years. We apply the target multiple to 2030E earnings to capture the growth trajectory of the company.

Key risks. Key downside risks to our view and price target include: (1) decline in global volumes in onshore wind that would likely negatively impact order intake; (2) lower US installations, (3) the absence of M&A in the wind sector that could make our M&A component less meaningful; and (4) a significant decline in commodity prices that would likely make wind less profitable vs. thermal technologies.

The GS Factor Profile provides investment context for a stock by comparing key attributes to the market (i.e. our universe of rated stocks) and its sector peers. The four key attributes depicted are: Growth, Financial Returns, Multiple (e.g. valuation) and Integrated (a composite of Growth, Financial Returns and Multiple). Growth, Financial Returns and Multiple are calculated by using normalized ranks for specific metrics for each stock. The normalized ranks for the metrics are then averaged and converted into percentiles for the relevant attribute. The precise calculation of each metric may vary depending on the fiscal year, industry and region, but the standard approach is as follows:

Growth is based on a stock's forward-looking sales growth, EBITDA growth and EPS growth (for financial stocks, only EPS and sales growth), with a higher percentile indicating a higher growth company. Financial Returns is based on a stock's forward-looking ROE, ROCE and CROCI (for financial stocks, only ROE), with a higher percentile indicating a company with higher financial returns. Multiple is based on a stock's forward-looking P/E, P/B, price/dividend (P/D), EV/EBITDA, EV/FCF and EV/Debt Adjusted Cash Flow (DACF) (for financial stocks, only P/E, P/B and P/D), with a higher percentile indicating a stock trading at a higher multiple. The Integrated percentile is calculated as the average of the Growth percentile, Financial Returns percentile and (100% - Multiple percentile).

Financial Returns and Multiple use the GS analyst forecasts at the fiscal year-end at least three quarters in the future. Growth uses inputs for the fiscal year at least seven quarters in the future compared with the year at least three quarters in the future (on a per-share basis for all metrics).
For a more detailed description of how we calculate the GS Factor Profile, please contact your GS representative.

Across our global coverage, we examine stocks using an M&A framework, considering both qualitative factors and quantitative factors (which may vary across sectors and regions) to incorporate the potential that certain companies could be acquired. We then assign a M&A rank as a means of scoring companies under our rated coverage from 1 to 3, with 1 representing high (30%-50%) probability of the company becoming an acquisition target, 2 representing medium (15%-30%) probability and 3 representing low (0%-15%) probability. For companies ranked 1 or 2, in line with our standard departmental guidelines we incorporate an M&A component into our target price. M&A rank of 3 is considered immaterial and therefore does not factor into our price target, and may or may not be discussed in research.

paragraph_content.content: Buy (B), Neutral (N), Sell (S) Analysts recommend stocks as Buys or Sells for inclusion on various regional Investment Lists. Being assigned a Buy or Sell on an Investment List is determined by a stock's total return potential relative to its coverage universe. Any stock not assigned as a Buy or a Sell on an Investment List with an active rating (i.e., a stock that is not Rating Suspended, Not Rated, Early-Stage Biotech, Coverage Suspended or Not Covered), is deemed Neutral. Each region manages Regional Conviction Lists, which are selected from Buy rated stocks on the respective region's Investment Lists and represent investment recommendations focused on the size of the total return potential and/or the likelihood of the realization of the return across their respective areas of coverage. The addition or removal of stocks from such Conviction Lists are managed by the Investment Review Committee or other designated committee in each respective region and do not represent a change in the analysts' investment rating for such stocks.

Total return potential represents the upside or downside differential between the current share price and the price target, including all paid or anticipated dividends, expected during the time horizon associated with the price target. Price targets are required for all covered stocks. The total return potential, price target and associated time horizon are stated in each report adding or reiterating an Investment List membership.
Coverage Universe: A list of all stocks in each coverage universe is available by primary analyst, stock and coverage universe at https://www.gs.com/research/hedge.html.
